content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published the Housing and Health Guidelines in 2018, with the ISBN 978-92-4-155037-6. These guidelines are distributed under a Creative Commons license, allowing users to copy, redistribute, and adapt the content for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guidelines emphasize the critical impact of housing quality on public health, particularly in urban areas where the population is expected to double by 2050, increasing the demand for housing. Poor housing conditions are linked to significant health risks, and improving these conditions can save lives, reduce disease, enhance quality of life, alleviate poverty, and contribute to achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as SDG 3 (health) and SDG 11 (sustainable cities). Housing is identified as a key entry point for intersectoral public health programs and primary prevention efforts. The WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations on housing conditions and interventions that promote health and safety. They aim to guide national, regional, and local governments in setting housing standards and regulations. By addressing housing as a sector rather than focusing on specific health risks or policies, the guidelines integrate existing WHO guidance with new evidence-based recommendations. This approach facilitates the inclusion of health considerations in housing, energy, community development, and urban planning policies. The guidelines also support countries in developing tools and strategies to translate housing standards into actionable national policies. WHO collaborates with a broad network of international partners, including its regional and country offices, ministries of health, building and construction authorities, collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies (such as UN-Habitat), and non-governmental organizations. Raising housing standards is seen as a critical pathway to improving health and well-being for all. The development of these guidelines was coordinated by Nathalie Röbbel under the supervision of Carlos Dora and Eugenio Villar from the WHO Department of Public Health, Environmental, and Social Determinants of Health. Contributions were made by various WHO departments, regional offices, and external experts, including the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and the External Review Group (ERG). The guidelines underwent extensive review and input from these groups, ensuring a comprehensive and evidence-based approach. The guidelines also include systematic reviews on topics such as insulation against cold, indoor cold, housing safety and injuries, indoor heat, household crowding, and accessible home environments for individuals with functional impairments. These reviews were conducted by experts from various institutions worldwide, ensuring a robust evidence base for the recommendations. WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous individuals and organizations in the development of these guidelines, including technical reviewers, administrative support staff, and interns. Special thanks are extended to those who provided methodological support, technical input, and assistance in drafting and finalizing the document. The guidelines aim to serve as a valuable resource for improving housing conditions and promoting health globally.
